title: L'Alfabeto e la Pronuncia
subtitle: Italian spelling is famously regular — learn the handful of rules that make it so.
objectives: Say the 21 letters of the Italian alphabet
Pronounce c/g before different vowels correctly
Recognize gn, gl and sc as single sounds

content.intro: Italian is written almost exactly as it sounds. Once you know a small set of spelling rules, you can read any Italian word aloud correctly — even one you've never seen.
content.explanation:
The Italian alphabet has 21 native letters (no j, k, w, x, y — these appear only in loanwords like jeans or whisky). Every vowel (a, e, i, o, u) is always pronounced clearly and the same way — Italian has no silent vowels and no vowel reduction like English “the” becoming “thuh”.

The trickiest part for English speakers is that c and g change sound depending on the letter that follows them, and a few two/three-letter combinations represent a single sound.

rules.heading: a) C and G before vowels
rules.body:
• ca, co, cu = hard "k" sound — casa, cosa, cubo
  • ce, ci = soft "ch" sound (like English "cheese") — cena, cinema
  • ga, go, gu = hard "g" sound — gatto, gonna, guanto
  • ge, gi = soft "j" sound (like English "jet") — gelato, giorno

rules.heading: b) Keeping the hard/soft sound before e or i
rules.body:
• Add an h to keep the hard sound before e/i: che, chi = "k" (chi, "who"); ghe, ghi = hard "g" (spaghetti)
  • Add an i to keep the soft sound before a/o/u: cia, cio, ciu = "ch" (ciao); gia, gio, giu = "j" (giorno) — the i is silent here, just a spelling signal

rules.heading: c) Special combinations
rules.body:
• gn = "ny" as in canyon — gnocchi, bagno
  • gli = "ly" as in million — famiglia, figlio
  • sc before e/i = "sh" — pesce, sciare; before a/o/u = "sk" — scuola, pesca
  • Double consonants are held longer than single ones — sono (I am) vs. sonno (sleep) are genuinely different words

examples.en: Hi, what's your name? — ciao starts with the soft "ch" sound
I'm hungry, I want pasta — voglio has a soft "ly"-like gli is not here, but voglio's gli combo shows the pattern in famiglia
The cat sleeps on the bed — gatto has the hard "g" sound
My daughter studies at university — figlia uses the gli "ly" sound
The spaghetti is delicious — spaghetti keeps the hard "g" thanks to the h

commonMistakes.why: ci before a vowel is always the soft "ch" sound in Italian, unlike the hard c English speakers expect.

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating "sono" and "sonno" as the same word
commonMistakes.right: sono (I am / they are) vs. sonno (sleep, drowsiness) — genuinely different
commonMistakes.why: Double consonants change the meaning of the word, not just the spelling — they must be held longer in speech.

items.prompt: How is the "c" in "cena" (dinner) pronounced?
items.explanation: Ce/ci is always the soft "ch" sound in Italian.

items.prompt: How is the "gn" in "bagno" (bathroom) pronounced?
items.explanation: gn is always a single "ny" sound, never two separate letters.

items.prompt: Which word has the hard "g" sound?
items.explanation: Ga/go/gu is hard; ge/gi is soft — gatto has ga, the hard sound.

exercises.title: Match the Spelling to Its Sound

items.explanation: The h and i in these combinations are silent spelling signals, not pronounced letters of their own.

items.prompt: How is the "g" in "gelato" pronounced?
items.explanation: Ge/gi is always the soft "j" sound.

items.prompt: How is the "sc" in "scuola" pronounced?
items.explanation: Before a/o/u, sc is the hard "sk" sound; only before e/i is it "sh".

items.prompt: Which word has the soft "ch" sound (like English "ch" in cheese)?
items.explanation: Ce/ci is soft; chiesa keeps a hard "k" thanks to the h.

items.prompt: How is "gli" in "famiglia" pronounced?
items.explanation: Gli is always a single "ly" sound.

items.prompt: Which word keeps the hard "g" sound before "i"?
items.explanation: The h in ghi keeps the hard "g" sound before i.

items.prompt: Which pair of words are genuinely different because of a double consonant?
items.explanation: Sono (I am) and sonno (sleep) are different words; the double n must be held longer.

items.prompt: How is "qu" pronounced in "quattro"?
items.explanation: Qu in Italian is pronounced "kw", same as in English "queen".

items.prompt: Which word has the soft "j" sound?
items.explanation: Gi before a vowel is the soft "j" sound; gatto and gonna keep the hard g.

items.prompt: How is "z" typically pronounced in "pizza"?
items.explanation: Italian z is most often pronounced "ts", as in pizza.

items.prompt: Which combination produces the "sh" sound?
items.explanation: Sc before e/i is the "sh" sound; before a/o/u it's "sk".

exercises.title: Complete the Spelling
exercises.instructions: Fill in the letter or letters that produce the described sound.

items.prompt: The word for "who" is written ___i (needs the hard "k" sound before i).
items.explanation: Adding h keeps the hard "k" sound before i: chi.

items.prompt: "Spaghetti" keeps its hard "g" sound thanks to the letter ___ before "etti".
items.explanation: The h in ghe/ghi keeps the hard "g" sound before e/i.

items.prompt: "Giorno" keeps its soft "j" sound thanks to the silent letter ___ before "orno".
items.explanation: The silent i in gio/gia/giu keeps the soft "j" sound before a/o/u.

items.prompt: The bathroom word "bagno" contains the combination ___, pronounced "ny".
items.explanation: Gn is always pronounced "ny", as in canyon.

items.prompt: "Family" in Italian, famiglia, contains the combination ___, pronounced "ly".
items.explanation: Gli is always the "ly" sound.

items.prompt: "Fish", pesce, uses ___ before e for the "sh" sound.
items.explanation: Sc before e/i is the "sh" sound.

items.prompt: "School", scuola, uses sc before ___ for the hard "sk" sound.
items.explanation: Sc before a/o/u is the hard "sk" sound.

items.prompt: "Sleep", sonno, is spelled with a double ___, held longer than in sono (I am).
items.explanation: The double n changes the meaning entirely.

items.prompt: "Quanto" (how much) starts with the combination ___, pronounced "kw".
items.explanation: Qu is always pronounced "kw" in Italian, same as English "queen".

items.prompt: "Zio" (uncle) starts with the letter ___, usually pronounced "ts".
items.explanation: Italian z is most often pronounced "ts".

items.statement: Ge and gi are always pronounced with a hard "g" sound.
items.explanation: Ge/gi are the soft "j" sound; ghe/ghi keep the hard sound.

items.statement: Adding an h after c or g keeps the hard sound before e or i.
items.explanation: Che/chi and ghe/ghi keep the hard "k"/"g" sounds.

items.statement: Sc before a, o or u is pronounced "sh".
items.explanation: Sc before a/o/u is "sk"; "sh" is only before e/i.

items.statement: Double consonants in Italian are pronounced exactly like single consonants.
items.explanation: Double consonants are held noticeably longer and can change the word's meaning.

items.statement: Gn is pronounced as two separate sounds, "g" then "n".
items.explanation: Gn is always a single "ny" sound.

items.statement: Gli is pronounced "ly", as in the English word "million".
items.explanation: Gli is always the "ly" sound.

items.statement: Every Italian vowel is pronounced clearly, with no reduction like English "the" becoming "thuh".
items.explanation: Italian vowels are always pronounced fully and clearly.

items.statement: The Italian alphabet includes the letters j, k, w, x and y as native letters.
items.explanation: These only appear in loanwords like jeans or whisky, not native Italian words.

items.statement: Qu is always pronounced "kw", the same as in English "queen".
items.explanation: Qu keeps the "kw" sound in Italian, just as in English.

items.statement: Z is always silent in Italian.
items.explanation: Z is usually pronounced "ts", as in pizza, never silent.

items.statement: Ci before a vowel (as in ciao) is the soft "ch" sound.
items.explanation: Ci before a vowel keeps the soft "ch" sound.

items.statement: Ca, co and cu are all pronounced with the soft "ch" sound.
items.explanation: Ca/co/cu are the hard "k" sound; only ce/ci are soft.

summary: Every Italian vowel is pronounced clearly — there is no vowel reduction.
C/g are hard before a, o, u and soft before e, i; h keeps them hard, i keeps them soft.
gn = "ny", gli = "ly", sc(e/i) = "sh" — and double consonants are genuinely held longer.
